prompt:
You have SOLD one European call option and must hedge it.

The stock starts at 100; the strike is 100; maturity is T = 0.5 years; the risk-free rate is r = 0; the volatility is sigma = 0.3 and it is the same volatility the option was priced with, so a free, continuous hedge would leave exactly zero risk and zero profit. You received the Black-Scholes premium up front.

You hedge by holding shares of the stock. Time is cut into 126 equal decision times. At a decision time you may trade to the Black-Scholes delta. Every trade costs c = 0.01 of the traded value (c x price x number of shares). At maturity your shares are settled to what delivery needs, and that last trade pays the cost too.

Your policy is scored on many simulated price paths you cannot see:
    J = E[total transaction cost] + lam x std(terminal profit and loss),   lam = 2
Lower is better. Trading more often lowers the std but raises the cost; the aim is the best balance.

YOUR CHOICE: an integer interval m between 1 and 63. You look at your hedge only at every m-th decision time (and at the start); when you look, you trade to the Black-Scholes delta.

Finish your reply with exactly one line:
  policy: interval=<integer>
Worked example of the format:
  policy: interval=5

The stock starts at 100; the strike is 100; maturity is T = 0.5 years; the risk-free rate is r = 0.02; the volatility is sigma = 0.2 and it is the same volatility the option was priced with, so a free, continuous hedge would leave exactly zero risk and zero profit. You received the Black-Scholes premium up front.

You hedge by holding shares of the stock. Time is cut into 126 equal decision times. At a decision time you may trade to the Black-Scholes delta. Every trade costs c = 0.01 of the traded value (c x price x number of shares). At maturity your shares are settled to what delivery needs, and that last trade pays the cost too.

Your policy is scored on many simulated price paths you cannot see:
    J = E[total transaction cost] + lam x std(terminal profit and loss),   lam = 2
Lower is better. Trading more often lowers the std but raises the cost; the aim is the best balance.

YOUR CHOICE: a no-trade band that may depend on the state. At every decision time you trade to the Black-Scholes delta only if your holding differs from it by MORE than band(gamma, S, tau), where gamma is the option's gamma, S the current stock price and tau the time left to maturity. The result is clipped to [0, 1].

Allowed: + - * / **, exp, log, sqrt, abs, maximum, minimum, pi, the variables gamma, S, tau, and the constants c, lam, sigma, r, T (use their names).

Finish your reply with exactly one line:
  band(gamma,S,tau) = <expression>
Worked example of the format (a constant band):
  band(gamma,S,tau) = 0.03

Hint: a band that is the same everywhere is easy; a band that reacts to gamma and to the cost c can do better.
